topic.title: Gradients of perpendicular lines and equations of perpendiculars
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: One 4-mark question in every M4 paper read (Summer 2023 Q16, Summer 2024 Q17, November 2024 Q17, Summer 2025 Q14, November 2025 Q18, Summer 2026 Q15), always in the middle third of the paper. The harder versions give the line as ax + by = c, or ask for a missing coordinate rather than an equation.
mustMemorise: Perpendicular gradient = −1/m; equivalently the two gradients multiply to −1
Rearrange to y = mx + c before reading m, dividing every term
Substitute the given point into y = mx + c to find c, then write the whole equation
Gradient between two points = (change in y) ÷ (change in x), taken in the same order
The diagonals of a rhombus (and of a square) bisect each other at right angles
A perpendicular bisector needs the midpoint as well as the perpendicular gradient
notOnThisSpec: The vector form or the equation of a line in three dimensions (A level, not GCSE)
Distance from a point to a line as a formula (not on this specification)
The equation of a tangent to a circle at a given point is M8-NA, not M4: this statement is about perpendicular gradients themselves

note.title: Perpendicular lines
note.subject: maths

mustKnow: y = mx + c, and the gradient between two points = (change in y) ÷ (change in x)
Midpoint of a segment = the average of the x-coordinates and the average of the y-coordinates

notOnThisSpec: The vector form or the equation of a line in three dimensions (A level, not GCSE)
Distance from a point to a line as a formula (not on this specification)

mustBeAbleTo: Write down the gradient of a line perpendicular to a given line, from a whole number, a fraction or a negative fraction
Rearrange ax + by = c into y = mx + c, dividing every term, and read the gradient
Find the equation of the line through a given point perpendicular to a given line, and write the whole equation
Find a gradient from two coordinates, including when one coordinate is negative
Use the equation of the perpendicular as a tool: substitute a known coordinate to find a missing one
Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of a segment, using the midpoint
Use the fact that the diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles to find the equation of the second diagonal
Show that two given lines are perpendicular by finding both gradients and their product
sheet.howExamined: M4 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks). One question every series, 4 marks, single part, placed between Q14 and Q18: Summer 2023 Q16, Summer 2024 Q17, November 2024 Q17, Summer 2025 Q14, November 2025 Q18, Summer 2026 Q15. Half of them print the line in the form ax + by = c so that it must be rearranged first. The scheme is A1 for the perpendicular gradient, MA1 for the substitution of the point, MA1 for c and A1 for the finished equation; when the question asks for a missing coordinate instead, the last two marks move to forming the equation and substituting the known coordinate.
traps: Reading the gradient before rearranging: from 3x + 2y = 7 the gradient is not 3 (Summer 2024 M4 Q17, where many scored zero)
Changing the sign without turning the fraction over, or turning it over without changing the sign (Summer 2025 M4 Q14)
Stopping at the perpendicular gradient and never substituting the point, so c is missing (November 2024 M4 Q17, Summer 2025 M4 Q14)
Inventing a gradient from coordinates printed in the question that are not both on the given line — no follow-through is allowed from it (Summer 2023 M4 Q16)
Finding both gradients in a missing-coordinate question and stalling, instead of writing the equation and substituting (November 2025 M4 Q18)
Substituting an end point instead of the midpoint in a perpendicular bisector
Dividing only the constant when rearranging, so −4y = −3x + 12 becomes y = −3/4 x − 3

steps.decision: The gradient can only be read once the equation is in the form y = mx + c. I make y the subject first: subtract 4x from both sides, then divide every term by 3.

options: Because the number in front of x is only the gradient when y is alone on one side
Because 4x + 3y = 24 is not the equation of a straight line
Because the gradient is always the largest number in the equation
whyMenu.explain: y = mx + c is the only arrangement in which the coefficient of x is the gradient. Reading 4 straight off 4x + 3y = 24 gives the wrong line.

steps.decision: Both terms were divided by 3, so the coefficient of x is −4/3, not −4. I write it down before touching the perpendicular.
Turn the fraction upside down and change the sign: the negative reciprocal of −4/3 is 3/4. A quick check: (−4/3) × (3/4) = −1.

options: Because the gradients of two perpendicular lines multiply to give −1
Because perpendicular lines always have positive gradients
Because you always swap the sign and leave the fraction alone
whyMenu.explain: Perpendicular gradients multiply to −1, so the second gradient is −1 divided by the first: the negative reciprocal.

steps.decision: The gradient alone is not an equation. Substituting the given point into y = mx + c is the only step that uses the coordinates, and it is where the examiners say candidates stop.
Write the finished equation, not just c. Multiplying through by 4 clears the fractions if you prefer whole numbers; both forms are accepted.

twin.stem: Find the equation of the line through $(4,\ -1)$ that is perpendicular to $5x + 2y = 14$.

workedExamples.stem: Line $L$ passes through $A(-2,\ 1)$ and $B(6,\ 5)$. Line $K$ is perpendicular to $L$ and also passes through $B$. The point $(t,\ 3)$ lies on $K$. Find the value of $t$.

steps.decision: Change in y over change in x, taking the points in the same order top and bottom. Subtracting −2 adds 2, which is where sign slips happen.

B is on K, so its coordinates satisfy the equation of K. The examiners' note on this question is that most candidates had both gradients and then stopped: the equation is the tool that answers the question.

options: Because a coordinate cannot be found from a gradient alone
Because every line must be written in the form y = mx + c
Because B is the midpoint of K
whyMenu.explain: A gradient describes a direction; only the equation ties x and y together so an unknown coordinate can be found.

steps.decision: Substitute the known coordinate, here y = 3, and solve the linear equation. Adding 2t to both sides keeps every number positive.

steps.working: $3y = x + 9 \Rightarrow y = \tfrac{1}{3}x + 3$, so the gradient of $PR$ is $\frac{1}{3}$
steps.decision: Divide every term by 3, including the 9. The gradient is 1/3, not 1.

steps.working: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles, so the gradient of $QS = -3$
steps.decision: This is the geometry fact that unlocks the question: all four sides equal means the diagonals are perpendicular bisectors of each other. Negative reciprocal of 1/3 is −3.

options: Because the diagonals of a rhombus meet at right angles
Because the diagonals of a rhombus are equal in length
Because a rhombus is a rectangle
whyMenu.explain: Equal sides force the diagonals to bisect each other at right angles. Equal diagonals is the rectangle property, which is a different shape.

steps.working: $M(3,\ 4)$ lies on both diagonals: $4 = -3(3) + c \Rightarrow c = 13$
steps.decision: The crossing point is on QS as well as on PR, so it is the point to substitute. Check it really is on PR first: 3(4) = 3 + 9.
Write the equation out. A quick check: at x = 3, −3(3) + 13 = 4, which is M.

items.stem: What is the gradient of a line perpendicular to $y = 3x - 7$?
items.skill: Take the negative reciprocal of a whole-number gradient

options.feedback: Turn 3 upside down to get 1/3 and change the sign. Check: 3 × (−1/3) = −1.
That is the gradient of a parallel line. Perpendicular needs the sign changed and the fraction turned over.
The sign has changed but the fraction has not been turned over. 3 × (−3) = −9, not −1.
The fraction has been turned over but the sign is still positive. 3 × 1/3 = 1, not −1.

items.stem: What is the gradient of the line $2x + 5y = 20$?
items.skill: Rearrange to y = mx + c before reading the gradient

options.feedback: 5y = −2x + 20, so y = −2/5 x + 4. Every term was divided by 5.
That is the coefficient of x before the equation was rearranged. The gradient can only be read once y is alone.
The sign is right but the division by 5 has not been done. Divide every term, including the 2x.
The fraction has been turned over. Rearranging gives −2/5; the reciprocal belongs to the perpendicular, not to this line.

items.stem: A line has gradient $-\frac{5}{2}$. What is the gradient of a line perpendicular to it?
items.skill: Negative reciprocal of a negative fraction

options.feedback: Turn it over to get −2/5, then change the sign to +2/5. Check: (−5/2) × (2/5) = −1.
The fraction has been turned over but the sign kept. Two negative gradients multiply to a positive number, so they cannot be perpendicular.
Only the sign has changed. The fraction has to be turned over as well.
That is the original gradient, which describes a parallel line.

items.stem: A line with gradient $4$ passes through $(2,\ 3)$. What is the value of $c$ in $y = 4x + c$?
items.skill: Substitute a point to find the intercept

options.feedback: The 8 has been added instead of subtracted. From 3 = 8 + c, take 8 from both sides.
That is the y-coordinate of the point. It is only the intercept when the x-coordinate is 0.
That is the x-coordinate. Substitute both coordinates into y = 4x + c and solve for c.

items.stem: A line passes through $(-3,\ 8)$ and $(5,\ 4)$. What is its gradient?
items.skill: Gradient from two points, with a negative coordinate

options.feedback: The difference in x has been divided by the difference in y. Gradient is change in y over change in x.
The size is right but the minus has been lost: y falls from 8 to 4 as x increases, so the gradient is negative.
The change in x has been taken as 5 − 3 = 2 instead of 5 − (−3) = 8. Subtracting a negative adds.

items.skill: Recognise a perpendicular line from its equation

options.feedback: (−1/4) × 4 = −1, so the two lines meet at right angles.
(−1/4) × (−4) = +1. Both gradients are negative, so both lines slope the same way.
(−1/4) × (1/4) is not −1. Only the sign was changed; the fraction must be turned over too.
Same gradient, different intercept: that is a parallel line, not a perpendicular one.

items.stem: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at $(6,\ 2)$. One diagonal has gradient $\frac{2}{3}$. What is the equation of the other diagonal?
items.skill: Use the right-angle property of a rhombus and substitute the crossing point

options.feedback: Perpendicular gradient −3/2, then 2 = −3/2(6) + c gives c = 11.
That is the first diagonal itself. The other diagonal is perpendicular to it.
The gradient is right but the crossing point was never substituted, so c is missing.
The y-coordinate of the crossing point has been used as c. It is only c when x = 0; here x = 6.

parts.stem: Write down the gradient of a line perpendicular to $y = 2x + 7$.
hints: The gradient of the given line is 2.
Turn 2 into the fraction 2/1, then invert and change the sign.
parts.workedSolution: The gradient of the given line is $2$. The negative reciprocal is $-\frac{1}{2}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The gradient of the given line was used, or only its sign was changed. Perpendicular means negative reciprocal: turn the fraction over and change the sign, then check that the two gradients multiply to −1.

parts.stem: Write down the gradient of a line perpendicular to $y = -\frac{3}{4}x + 2$.
hints: Turn −3/4 upside down.
Then change the sign.
parts.workedSolution: Inverting $-\tfrac{3}{4}$ gives $-\tfrac{4}{3}$; changing the sign gives $\frac{4}{3}$. Check: $-\tfrac{3}{4} \times \tfrac{4}{3} = -1$.

commonErrors.feedback: The gradient of the given line was used, or only its sign was changed. Perpendicular means negative reciprocal: turn the fraction over and change the sign, then check that the two gradients multiply to −1.

parts.stem: Find the gradient of the line $2x + 5y = 20$.

scheme.for: rearranged to y = −2/5 x + 4 (or 5y = −2x + 20 followed by division by 5)

hints: Subtract 2x from both sides.
Divide every term by 5, including the 2x.
parts.workedSolution: $2x + 5y = 20 \Rightarrow 5y = -2x + 20 \Rightarrow y = -\frac{2}{5}x + 4$, so the gradient is $-\frac{2}{5}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The gradient was read before the equation was rearranged. Make y the subject first, dividing every term, and only then take the negative reciprocal. No follow-through is allowed from a gradient that is not the correct one or its negative reciprocal.

parts.stem: Find the gradient of a line perpendicular to $3x - 4y = 12$.

scheme.for: rearranged to y = 3/4 x − 3, so the gradient of the given line is 3/4

hints: −4y = −3x + 12; dividing by −4 changes both signs.
Then invert and change the sign.
parts.workedSolution: $3x - 4y = 12 \Rightarrow -4y = -3x + 12 \Rightarrow y = \frac{3}{4}x - 3$. The gradient is $\frac{3}{4}$, so a perpendicular line has gradient $-\frac{4}{3}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The gradient was read before the equation was rearranged. Make y the subject first, dividing every term, and only then take the negative reciprocal. No follow-through is allowed from a gradient that is not the correct one or its negative reciprocal.
Dividing −4y = −3x + 12 by −4 makes the x term positive: y = 3/4 x − 3. Both signs on the right change, not just the constant.

parts.stem: Find the equation of the line that passes through $(0,\ 6)$ and is perpendicular to $y = \frac{1}{2}x$.

scheme.for: y = −2x + 6 (c read straight from the point on the y-axis)

hints: The negative reciprocal of 1/2 is −2.
The point has x = 0, so its y-coordinate is c.
parts.workedSolution: The perpendicular gradient is $-2$. Since $x = 0$ at the given point, $c = 6$ directly, so the line is $y = -2x + 6$.

commonErrors.feedback: The gradient earns the first mark. The point (0, 6) is on the y-axis, so c = 6 without any substitution; leaving c out loses the accuracy mark.

questions.solutionProgram: perp(1/2) = -2; point (0,6) on the y-axis so c = 6; y = -2x + 6; check x=0 -> y=6

parts.stem: Find the equation of the line that passes through $(4,\ -1)$ and is perpendicular to $y = 2x + 9$.
hints: Negative reciprocal of 2.
Substitute x = 4 and y = −1 into y = mx + c.
Write the finished equation, not just c.
parts.workedSolution: Gradient $= -\frac{1}{2}$. Substituting: $-1 = -\frac{1}{2}(4) + c = -2 + c$, so $c = 1$ and the line is $y = -\frac{1}{2}x + 1$.

commonErrors.feedback: The perpendicular gradient is correct, and that is the first mark. The remaining marks are for substituting the given point into y = mx + c, finding c and writing the whole equation.

parts.stem: Find the equation of the line that passes through $(-3,\ 7)$ and is perpendicular to $y = -\frac{1}{5}x + 4$.
hints: The negative reciprocal of −1/5 is 5.
5 × (−3) is −15, so c is larger than 7.
parts.workedSolution: Gradient $= 5$. Then $7 = 5(-3) + c = -15 + c$, so $c = 22$ and the line is $y = 5x + 22$.

commonErrors.feedback: The gradient mark is earned. In 7 = 5(−3) + c the product is −15, so c = 7 + 15 = 22. Adding instead of subtracting is the usual slip when the coordinate is negative.

parts.stem: Find the equation of the line that passes through $(6,\ 2)$ and is perpendicular to $3x + 2y = 8$.
hints: 2y = −3x + 8, then divide every term by 2.
Invert −3/2 and change the sign.
Substitute (6, 2).
parts.workedSolution: $3x + 2y = 8 \Rightarrow y = -\frac{3}{2}x + 4$, gradient $-\frac{3}{2}$. Perpendicular gradient $\frac{2}{3}$. Then $2 = \frac{2}{3}(6) + c = 4 + c$, so $c = -2$ and the line is $y = \frac{2}{3}x - 2$.

commonErrors.feedback: The gradient was read before the equation was rearranged. Make y the subject first, dividing every term, and only then take the negative reciprocal. No follow-through is allowed from a gradient that is not the correct one or its negative reciprocal.

parts.stem: Find the equation of the line that passes through $(-4,\ 9)$ and is perpendicular to $5y - 2x = 15$.
hints: Add 2x to both sides, then divide every term by 5.
The given gradient is 2/5.
parts.workedSolution: $5y - 2x = 15 \Rightarrow 5y = 2x + 15 \Rightarrow y = \frac{2}{5}x + 3$. Perpendicular gradient $-\frac{5}{2}$. Then $9 = -\frac{5}{2}(-4) + c = 10 + c$, so $c = -1$ and the line is $y = -\frac{5}{2}x - 1$.

commonErrors.feedback: Two marks for the rearrangement and the perpendicular gradient. Then −5/2 × (−4) = +10, not −10, so c = 9 − 10 = −1. Two negatives multiply to a positive.

parts.stem: A line passes through $(-1,\ 8)$ and $(5,\ -4)$. Find the gradient of a line perpendicular to it.
hints: Change in y over change in x, in the same order top and bottom.
parts.workedSolution: Gradient $= \dfrac{-4 - 8}{5 - (-1)} = \dfrac{-12}{6} = -2$, so a perpendicular line has gradient $\frac{1}{2}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The two differences have been used the other way round: gradient is change in y over change in x. Here that is −12 ÷ 6 = −2, and the perpendicular gradient is +1/2.

parts.stem: $A$ is the point $(2,\ -5)$ and $B$ is the point $(8,\ 3)$. Find the equation of the line through $B$ that is perpendicular to $AB$.
hints: Work out the gradient of AB first.
8/6 simplifies to 4/3.
The new line passes through B, so substitute (8, 3).
parts.workedSolution: Gradient of $AB = \dfrac{3 - (-5)}{8 - 2} = \dfrac{8}{6} = \frac{4}{3}$. Perpendicular gradient $-\frac{3}{4}$. Then $3 = -\frac{3}{4}(8) + c = -6 + c$, so $c = 9$ and the line is $y = -\frac{3}{4}x + 9$.

commonErrors.feedback: The perpendicular gradient is correct, and that is the first mark. The remaining marks are for substituting the given point into y = mx + c, finding c and writing the whole equation.

parts.stem: Show that the lines $y = 4x - 3$ and $x + 4y = 12$ are perpendicular.

expectedOrder: 4 x (-1/4) = -1 so the lines are perpendicular

scheme.for: second equation rearranged to y = −1/4x + 3, gradient −1/4
product of gradients shown to be −1, with the conclusion stated
scheme.examinerNote: The product must be seen; stating that one gradient is the negative reciprocal of the other, with both gradients written, is also accepted.

hints: Rearrange the second equation to y = mx + c.
Multiply the two gradients together.
Say what the answer −1 tells you.
parts.workedSolution: $x + 4y = 12 \Rightarrow 4y = -x + 12 \Rightarrow y = -\frac{1}{4}x + 3$. The gradients are $4$ and $-\frac{1}{4}$, and $4 \times -\frac{1}{4} = -1$, so the lines are perpendicular.

commonErrors.feedback: Show that means the reasoning is the answer. Both gradients and the product −1 must appear on the page; a bare statement earns nothing.

parts.stem: Line $L$ passes through $(1,\ 2)$ and $(7,\ 5)$. Line $K$ is perpendicular to $L$ and passes through $(7,\ 5)$. The point $(k,\ 7)$ lies on $K$. Find the value of $k$.
hints: Find the gradient of L, then of K.
Use (7, 5) to find c for K.
Put y = 7 into the equation of K and solve for x.
parts.workedSolution: Gradient of $L = \dfrac{5-2}{7-1} = \frac{1}{2}$, so gradient of $K = -2$. Through $(7,5)$: $5 = -14 + c$, so $c = 19$ and $K$ is $y = -2x + 19$. Putting $y = 7$: $7 = -2k + 19$, so $2k = 12$ and $k = 6$.

commonErrors.feedback: The perpendicular gradient is correct, and that is the first mark. The remaining marks are for substituting the given point into y = mx + c, finding c and writing the whole equation.

parts.stem: $P$ is the point $(-1,\ 2)$ and $Q$ is the point $(5,\ 6)$. Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $PQ$.
hints: A perpendicular bisector cuts PQ in half and at right angles, so it needs the midpoint and the perpendicular gradient.
Midpoint: average the x-coordinates and the y-coordinates.
Substitute the midpoint, not P or Q.
parts.workedSolution: Midpoint of $PQ = \left(\dfrac{-1+5}{2},\ \dfrac{2+6}{2}\right) = (2,\ 4)$. Gradient of $PQ = \dfrac{6-2}{5-(-1)} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}$, so the perpendicular gradient is $-\frac{3}{2}$. Then $4 = -\frac{3}{2}(2) + c = -3 + c$, so $c = 7$ and the bisector is $y = -\frac{3}{2}x + 7$.

commonErrors.feedback: The midpoint is the first mark, not the answer. A bisector is a line: carry on to the perpendicular gradient and then substitute (2, 4) to find c.
The gradient marks are earned. P was substituted instead of the midpoint: 2 = −3/2(−1) + c gives the wrong c. A bisector passes through the middle of PQ.

parts.stem: Find the equation of the line through the point $(10,\ -3)$ that is perpendicular to $2x + 5y = 30$.

scheme.examinerNote: No follow-through from any gradient other than −2/5 or its negative reciprocal.

hints: Rearrange first: the gradient is not 2.
Divide every term by 5 when you make y the subject.
Substitute x = 10 and y = −3 into y = 5/2 x + c.
parts.workedSolution: $2x + 5y = 30 \Rightarrow 5y = -2x + 30 \Rightarrow y = -\frac{2}{5}x + 6$, so the gradient is $-\frac{2}{5}$ and the perpendicular gradient is $\frac{5}{2}$. Substituting $(10,\ -3)$: $-3 = \frac{5}{2}(10) + c = 25 + c$, so $c = -28$. The line is $y = \frac{5}{2}x - 28$.

commonErrors.feedback: The gradient was read before the equation was rearranged. Make y the subject first, dividing every term, and only then take the negative reciprocal. No follow-through is allowed from a gradient that is not the correct one or its negative reciprocal.
The perpendicular gradient is correct, and that is the first mark. The remaining marks are for substituting the given point into y = mx + c, finding c and writing the whole equation.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows the line $L$ through the points $A(-5,\ 4)$ and $B(3,\ 0)$.

Find the equation of the line that is perpendicular to $L$ and passes through $B$.
hints: Use the two coordinates printed in the question, not the squares on the grid.
B is on the x-axis, so its y-coordinate is 0.
Substitute (3, 0).
parts.workedSolution: Gradient of $L = \dfrac{0 - 4}{3 - (-5)} = \dfrac{-4}{8} = -\frac{1}{2}$, so the perpendicular gradient is $2$. Through $B(3,\ 0)$: $0 = 2(3) + c$, so $c = -6$ and the line is $y = 2x - 6$.

commonErrors.feedback: The gradient was counted off the grid rather than worked out from the coordinates. The diagram is not drawn accurately, so use (−5, 4) and (3, 0): −4 ÷ 8 = −1/2.

parts.stem: Write down the coordinates of the point where this perpendicular line crosses the $y$-axis.

scheme.for: (0, −6), follow through from the candidate's c

hints: A line crosses the y-axis where x = 0.
The y-intercept is the value of c.
parts.workedSolution: At the $y$-axis $x = 0$, so $y = c = -6$: the point is $(0,\ -6)$.

commonErrors.feedback: The coordinates are the other way round. On the y-axis the x-coordinate is 0, so the point is (0, −6). The pair (−6, 0) is where the line crosses the x-axis, and 3 is where it crosses there.

figures.alt: A rhombus ABCD with all four sides marked equal and both diagonals drawn as dashed lines meeting at a point M, where a right-angle square is marked.

parts.stem:
The diagonals of the rhombus $ABCD$ meet at $M(4,\ 5)$. The diagonal $AC$ has equation $x + 2y = 14$.

Find the equation of the diagonal $BD$.

scheme.for: gradient of BD = 2, because the diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles

hints: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles — that is what makes this a perpendicular question.
Rearrange x + 2y = 14 to read the gradient.
M is on both diagonals, so substitute (4, 5).
parts.workedSolution: $x + 2y = 14 \Rightarrow y = -\frac{1}{2}x + 7$, so the gradient of $AC$ is $-\frac{1}{2}$. The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular, so $BD$ has gradient $2$. $M(4,\ 5)$ lies on $BD$: $5 = 2(4) + c$, so $c = -3$ and $BD$ is $y = 2x - 3$.

commonErrors.feedback: The gradient was read before the equation was rearranged. Make y the subject first, dividing every term, and only then take the negative reciprocal. No follow-through is allowed from a gradient that is not the correct one or its negative reciprocal.
The perpendicular gradient is correct, and that is the first mark. The remaining marks are for substituting the given point into y = mx + c, finding c and writing the whole equation.

parts.stem: The vertex $D$ has coordinates $(7,\ 11)$. Find the coordinates of the vertex $B$.

scheme.for: uses that M is the midpoint of BD: 4 = (x + 7) ÷ 2 and 5 = (y + 11) ÷ 2

hints: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other, so M is the midpoint of BD.
Going from D to M changes x by −3 and y by −6; do the same again.
Check your point satisfies the equation of BD.
parts.workedSolution: The diagonals bisect each other, so $M$ is the midpoint of $BD$: $4 = \dfrac{x + 7}{2}$ gives $x = 1$, and $5 = \dfrac{y + 11}{2}$ gives $y = -1$. So $B = (1,\ -1)$, and it checks in $y = 2x - 3$: $2(1) - 3 = -1$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the midpoint of D and M, not the far vertex. M is already the midpoint of BD, so B is the same step again beyond M: from D(7, 11) to M(4, 5) is −3 and −6, so B is (1, −1).

methodLock.instruction: Find the equation of the diagonal BD
methodLock.requiredMethod: The perpendicular property of the rhombus diagonals, then substitution of M; measuring the diagram or guessing a second point earns nothing

context.setting: Two perpendicular lines L and K through given points

parts.stem:
Line $L$ passes through $P(-2,\ -3)$ and $Q(6,\ 1)$.

Find the gradient of $L$.
hints: Change in y over change in x.
parts.workedSolution: Gradient of $L = \dfrac{1 - (-3)}{6 - (-2)} = \dfrac{4}{8} = \frac{1}{2}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The differences have been swapped: 8 ÷ 4 instead of 4 ÷ 8. Gradient is always change in y over change in x, with the points taken in the same order on both lines of the fraction.

parts.stem: Line $K$ is perpendicular to $L$ and passes through $Q$. Find the equation of $K$.
hints: Negative reciprocal of your answer to part (a).
K passes through Q(6, 1).
Write the equation, not just c.
parts.workedSolution: Gradient of $K = -2$. Through $Q(6,\ 1)$: $1 = -2(6) + c = -12 + c$, so $c = 13$ and $K$ is $y = -2x + 13$.

commonErrors.feedback: The perpendicular gradient is correct, and that is the first mark. The remaining marks are for substituting the given point into y = mx + c, finding c and writing the whole equation.

parts.stem: The point $(t,\ 21)$ lies on $K$. Find the value of $t$.
hints: Substitute y = 21 into the equation of K.
Dividing 8 by −2 gives a negative answer.

commonErrors.feedback: The substitution mark is earned. From −2t = 8, dividing by −2 gives t = −4; a positive 4 would give y = 5, not 21. Substituting back is the quickest check.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh was asked to find the equation of the line through $(2,\ 5)$ perpendicular to $3x + 2y = 18$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The gradient was read from 3x + 2y = 18 while y was still tied up with a 2. Rearranging gives 2y = −3x + 18, then y = −3/2 x + 9, so the gradient is −3/2 and the perpendicular gradient is 2/3.
correction: 2y = −3x + 18, so y = −3/2 x + 9 and the gradient is −3/2
findTheMistake.feedback: Every line after the first is worked correctly, which makes this expensive: the scheme allows follow-through only from the correct gradient or its negative reciprocal, so nothing is earned. Make y the subject before you look for m, and divide every term when you do. Summer 2024 M4 Q17: many candidates scored zero here for exactly this reason.

findTheMistake.stem: Ciara was asked to find the equation of the line through $(8,\ 1)$ perpendicular to $y = 4x - 5$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Only the sign was changed. Perpendicular means negative reciprocal: turn 4 over to get 1/4 and then change the sign, giving −1/4. The test is that the two gradients multiply to −1, and 4 × (−4) = −16.
findTheMistake.feedback: The substitution and the arithmetic are sound, so the method you are carrying is right; it is the first line that costs everything, because the rest follows from it. Say the check out loud before you move on: the two gradients must multiply to −1. Summer 2025 M4 Q14: weaker candidates used the gradient itself or its reciprocal without the sign change.

findTheMistake.stem: Sean was asked to find the equation of the line through $(4,\ 9)$ perpendicular to the line $y = \frac{2}{3}x + 1$. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: A gradient was invented from the point in the question and the intercept of the printed line. Those two points are not both on the given line, so the number 2 belongs to no line at all. The gradient is already printed: it is 2/3.
correction: The given line is y = 2/3 x + 1, so its gradient is 2/3
findTheMistake.feedback: This is the error the Summer 2023 examiners singled out: coordinates printed in the question were combined into a gradient of their own, and no follow-through was allowed from it. Before you calculate anything, ask which line the gradient is supposed to describe; if the equation is given, read m from it.

prompts.prompt: The gradients of two perpendicular lines multiply to give what?
prompts.answer: $-1$. So if one gradient is $m$, the other is $-\dfrac{1}{m}$.

prompts.prompt: The four steps for finding the equation of a perpendicular line through a given point.
prompts.answer: 1 Rearrange the given line to $y = mx + c$ and read $m$. 2 Perpendicular gradient $= -\dfrac{1}{m}$. 3 Substitute the given point into $y = mx + c$ to find $c$. 4 Write the whole equation.

prompts.prompt: Why is the gradient of $3x + 2y = 18$ not $3$?
prompts.answer: Because $y$ is not on its own. Rearranged, $2y = -3x + 18$ and $y = -\tfrac{3}{2}x + 9$, so the gradient is $-\tfrac{3}{2}$. Every term is divided by 2, including the $3x$.

prompts.prompt: A line has gradient $-\dfrac{2}{7}$. What is the gradient of a perpendicular line?
prompts.answer: $\dfrac{7}{2}$. Turn it over and change the sign; check $-\tfrac{2}{7} \times \tfrac{7}{2} = -1$.

prompts.prompt: You have the perpendicular gradient and a point. What is the very next line of working?
prompts.answer: Substitute the point into $y = mx + c$ and solve for $c$. The examiners' note is that most candidates stop at the gradient; the remaining marks live in this line.

prompts.prompt: What is a perpendicular bisector, and what two things must you work out to find its equation?
prompts.answer: The line that cuts a segment in half and at right angles. You need the midpoint of the segment and the negative reciprocal of the segment's gradient.

prompts.prompt: The diagonals of a rhombus have what special relationship?
prompts.answer: They bisect each other at right angles, so their gradients multiply to $-1$ and the crossing point lies on both.

prompts.prompt: A question gives a line and a point, and you want the gradient. Where must the gradient come from?
prompts.answer: From the given line only. Building a gradient out of the point in the question and some other printed coordinate describes no line in the question, and no follow-through is allowed from it.

prompts.prompt: You have the equation of a perpendicular line and you are asked for a missing coordinate. What do you do?
prompts.answer: Substitute the coordinate you know into the equation and solve the resulting linear equation for the one you do not know.

prompts.prompt: A line through $(0,\ 7)$ is perpendicular to $y = \tfrac{1}{3}x - 2$. Write its equation without doing any substitution.
prompts.answer: $y = -3x + 7$. The point is on the $y$-axis, so its $y$-coordinate is $c$ directly.

findings.asked: Equation of a line perpendicular to a given line, through a given point.
findings.wentWrong: Only the more able started correctly, and they usually finished. Others did not know how to obtain the original gradient by substitution, and the commonest error was to use the two coordinates printed in the question to invent a gradient (7/6); no follow-through was allowed from a wrong gradient.
findings.rule: The gradient must come from the given line, not from unrelated points.

findings.asked: Perpendicular line when the original is not in the form y = mx + c.
findings.wentWrong: Many scored zero because they could not rearrange to read the gradient; follow-through only from the correct gradient or its negative reciprocal.
findings.rule: Rearrange to y = mx + c before reading m.

findings.asked: Perpendicular gradient, then the equation through given coordinates.
findings.wentWrong: Most found the perpendicular gradient but then could not find the equation; a wrong starting gradient usually meant zero.
findings.rule: Substitute the point into y = mx + c to find c.

findings.wentWrong: Improving each year; most knew the perpendicular gradient was -1/4. Weaker candidates used 4 or 1/4, and only the more able found c correctly.

findings.asked: Use a perpendicular to find a missing coordinate.
findings.wentWrong: Most got the gradient of L and its negative reciprocal, then stalled.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote the equation of the perpendicular line K first, then substituted the known y-value (23) to find the missing x.
findings.rule: Turn the gradient into an equation, then substitute what you know.

insight.ruleToRemember: Rearrange to y = mx + c; the perpendicular gradient is -1/m; substitute the given point to find c; then use that equation for whatever is asked.
insight.aStarSignal: Using the perpendicular's equation as a tool to find an unknown coordinate rather than as the final answer.
